title: Cato and the Grumblewart's Secret
markdown:
Elf Cato had a wit sharp as an icicle and eyes that could spy a forgotten berry from a mile high. His dearest companion was Pine, a grand wise owl whose hoots held more wisdom than an ancient library and whose sight caught every secret the world tried to hide.

One sun-drenched morning, air tasting of pine needles, Cato skipped to the mountain market: stalls of rocks that glittered like captured stars, wool softer than a cloud’s whisper, cheeses with personality. Between a merchant hawking glowing moss and another with wind chimes humming forgotten lullabies, Cato spotted it. Less a creature than a walking, grumbling mud-pie. Big sorrowful eyes blinked slowly. A low contented rumble vibrated through Cato’s boots.

A merchant recoiled as if the mud might invade. “Good heavens, what is that?”

“That,” squeaked a tiny gnome, darting like a nervous beetle, “is a Grumblewart! Nobody wants it. Too muddy. Too grumpy. Too Grumblewart-y.”

The market buzzed agreement. Too messy. Too strange. Cato saw a steady unbothered gaze, a being at home in its squishy skin. Grin drier than sun-baked stone: “I’ll take it.”

The market gasped. Pine, on Cato’s shoulder, a soft curious hoot. Certain?

“Absolutely.” A surprisingly gentle pat. “Character. Wonderful, boggy character.” He welcomed it home and bestowed a grand name: Bartholomew. Main talents: grumbling contentedly and a faint earthy aroma most villagers found challenging. They whispered, “Poor Cato.”

Then, as if by forgetfulness, a different gnome—just as wobbly, just as prone to dropping things—tumbled down Cato’s mountain path clutching a scroll tied with a rainbow-shimmer ribbon. “For you!” He gasped, got distracted by a sparkly rock, and ambled off humming tunelessly.

The scroll was a map, ink fine as spider-silk under moonlight, promising the legendary Sunstone Blossom: a bloom said to cure any ailment with a single warm glow. It showed every pebble, crack, twist of the ravine with breathtaking accuracy, and not a single helpful clue. No best way. No encouragement.

“This map,” Cato sighed, holding it for Pine, “is exactly right in every detail. Completely useless for getting anywhere.”

Pine hooted, thoughtful. It showed where, not how, and not why you should care.

Their adventure began. Perfect unhelpful precision led them into shadowy ravines. Air thin. Wind like lost spirits. The map pointed to a cliff so sheer the mountain seemed to have given up. “Right then.” Voice dry as toast. “The Sunstone Blossom is located precisely 3.7 feet to the left of that remarkably unsteady boulder. Splendid. HOW do we get there?”

A voice like a slow-motion avalanche. “Ho there! What’s all this grumbling?” Hob the ogre, enormous, towering over oldest trees, usually frowning, today a flicker of curiosity. Booming voice, gruff outside, heart soft as dew-kissed moss.

“We’re searching for the Sunstone Blossom, Hob. This map, while very detailed, is uncooperative.”

Hob squinted, massive brow furrowed. “Old Glimmer’s work. Precise as a glacier, helpful as a sieve in a sandstorm. He draws what is, not what you need.”

A tiny flash of iridescent colour: a Zizzwing, the sort that whispered secrets of rare plants if asked nicely. Cato pointed. “It might know where the Blossom is!”

Hob, bless his gigantic clumsy heart, decided to help. Thunderous: “HOO HOO! LITTLE BUG! DO YOU SEE THE PRETTY FLOWER?” The Zizzwing, startled by the earthquake-sized voice, zipped away like a panicked spark into mist.

“Oh, Hob.” Temples rubbed. “That was not a gentle inquiry. That was a demand delivered by sonic boom.” Straight face: “It’s not a prophecy. It’s a shopping list with an attitude problem.”

Pine, soaring, urgent sharp hoots. She swooped, wing pointing to a hidden alcove veiled by dripping moss. Cato followed.

There sat Bartholomew. Not just muddy. Glowing. Soft warm light pulsed from within, grumbles become gentle melodic hums. The thick muddy coat, once a mess, looked like a protective earthy shell holding healing power. Cato understood. The map was not a path to a blossom. It was a map to Bartholomew’s very specific, very special, very muddy resting place. The Grumblewart was the Sunstone Blossom—or rather, its quiet life-giving magic made visible.

Hob scratched his enormous chin, frown softening. “I’ll be a grumpy troll’s uncle. That grumbling mud-ball.”

Warmth more real than any clever remark. Bartholomew blinked mournful eyes, content. Pine landed softly. A hoot like a breath of wind, and no sermon required.

Back in the village a small child lay shivering, a cough no sweet tea could chase. Cato held Bartholomew at the bedside. The creature once dismissed as worthless let out a soft rumbling hum. Shivering stopped. Gentle warmth filled the room. The cough faded like a tiny shadow.

Villagers who had scoffed watched in silent awe. Bartholomew continued to grumble softly, and it sounded, to anyone who had been listening properly, like the most comforting melody on the mountain. Pine closed one eye, which in owl was applause. Cato, dry as ever, only said that the map had been right after all, which was the sort of joke that did not need explaining.
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing mountain adventure fantasy for ages 9-10
